title: Diagnose slow FMV playback when PS2 gameplay runs normally
summary: Compare one reproducible cutscene with nearby gameplay, verify emulation speed and audio drift, separate video decode or IPU behavior from general rendering load, and capture evidence without applying broad speed changes.
heroAlt: PCSX2 video and audio capture controls representing a focused FMV playback investigation

blocks.text: Use the cutscene boundary as a subsystem probe

When the same title reaches full speed in gameplay but slows only during a pre-rendered sequence, the device is not necessarily too weak for the game. PS2 FMV playback can exercise IPU decoding, color conversion, audio synchronization, software paths, and aspect switching differently from normal 3D rendering. Choose a cutscene reachable from a normal save and record the ten seconds before, the complete sequence, and the first gameplay after it.
Do not skip or fast-forward the measured cutscene, and do not enable unrelated cycle or speed controls. They can hide synchronization faults and invalidate the boundary comparison.

items: A normal save immediately before a cutscene that can be replayed.
A verified disc image and correct regional BIOS configuration.
Baseline renderer, driver, audio synchronization, and speed controls documented.
Emulation-speed and frame-time indicators captured with consistent overhead.
A second cutscene or title available if the first case is content-specific.

blocks.text: Compare gameplay, FMV, and return-to-game timing

items: 1. Cold-boot from the normal save and record stable gameplay immediately before the trigger.
2. Enter the cutscene without changing overlays or display orientation.
3. Mark emulation speed, visible cadence, audio drift, and the exact moment any slowdown begins.
4. Continue recording through the first gameplay segment after the FMV.
5. Replay with only the alternate stable renderer changed and compare the same timestamps.
6. Return to baseline and test the second cutscene to determine whether the symptom is title-wide.
7. Check logs for IPU, video, audio, or renderer messages near the transition.
8. Build a report containing the save location, timestamps, region, logs, and both renderer results.

blocks.text: A drop that begins precisely with video and ends precisely with gameplay isolates a path not heavily used by the surrounding scene. Audio that leads or trails over time adds synchronization evidence. If the slowdown continues after the cutscene, investigate thermal, cache, or general workload changes instead of labeling it FMV-only.
The evidence must show a repeatable difference at the content boundary while the general profile remains stable.

items: Gameplay before and after the cutscene reaches the expected speed.
The slowdown begins and ends at reproducible FMV timestamps.
Audio drift and visual cadence are documented separately.
Renderer comparison changes only one variable.
A second FMV indicates whether the issue is isolated or general.

blocks.text: Cases that need a cleaner reproduction

items: The save triggers random dialogue or alternate video: use a deterministic branch.
Capture overhead causes the slowdown: repeat with a lower-overhead timing method.
The device heats during a long intro: match temperature and shorten setup time.
The disc image reports read errors: verify storage before performance diagnosis.

blocks.text: Return the renderer, audio synchronization, aspect handling, and overlays to the recorded baseline, cold-boot the title, and replay the cutscene once without diagnostic capture. Preserve the save copy and concise report rather than leaving experimental speed changes enabled.
Not every cutscene is an FMV

Some sequences are rendered by the game engine and can share normal GS and CPU bottlenecks. Confirm that the boundary exercises a video path through logs, known title behavior, or the distinct timing pattern before using an FMV label.
